name: GraphRAG
question: Can retrieval answer questions about the whole corpus?
summary: GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph from the documents before any question arrives. An LLM extracts entities and relationships from every chunk, a clustering algorithm (Leiden) groups them into communities, and the LLM writes a summary of each community. Local search starts from entities named in the question and gathers their neighbours and source chunks, which helps multi-hop questions. Global search combines community summaries in a map-reduce step to answer questions about the whole corpus, such as the main themes, which vector search over single chunks answers poorly. Indexing costs far more than embedding, so many teams route only multi-hop and whole-corpus questions to the graph. This is corpus retrieval; a temporal graph of what an agent learns about users is Graph Memory in module 9.
useCases: Whole-corpus questions: themes, trends, “what are the main issues”
Multi-hop questions that join facts across documents
Investigations over reports, complaints or case files

steps.title: Set up a project
steps.text: Sahayak Telecom, a fictional operator, puts 5,000 outage and complaint reports into a GraphRAG project. The settings choose the chat and embedding models and the entity types: tower, vendor, circle, fault.

steps.title: Extract the graph
steps.text: Indexing sends every chunk to the LLM to pull out entities and relationships. This is the costly step, about ₹18,000 for this corpus, so it is tried on a 200-report sample first.

steps.title: Cluster and summarise
steps.text: Leiden clustering groups related entities into communities at several levels, and the LLM writes a report for each: “Pune circle, vendor X, repeated power faults”.

steps.title: Route by question type
steps.text: A small classifier sends simple fact questions to vector RAG, which is cheaper and just as good for them.

steps.title: Local or global
steps.text: Multi-hop questions go to local search, which walks entity neighbours. Whole-corpus questions go to global search, which maps over community reports and reduces the partial answers.

steps.title: Measure
steps.text: On 300 test questions, 30% of them about themes, vector RAG alone scores 59%; the routed setup scores 82%, at about ₹1,370 per 1,000 queries.

pros: Answers whole-corpus questions vector RAG cannot
Better multi-hop answers through entity relationships
Community reports are useful summaries on their own
Graph can be inspected and corrected
cons: Indexing needs an LLM pass over every chunk
Global queries are slow and costly
Incremental updates are harder than re-embedding
avoidWhen: Mostly single-fact lookups that vector RAG already answers
Fast-changing corpora with no budget to re-index

practice.scenario: Sahayak Telecom, a fictional operator, has 5,000 outage and complaint reports. Vector RAG answers single facts but fails on “what are the main causes of complaints in Pune this quarter?” and on joins such as “which vendors are linked to repeated tower outages?”. It builds a GraphRAG index once for about ₹18,000, then routes facts to vector RAG, multi-hop questions to local search and theme questions to global search. Answer quality on 300 test questions rises from 59% to 82%.

industries.use: Themes and root causes across outage and complaint reports
Links between claimants, garages, hospitals and agents in fraud reviews
Main positions across hundreds of consultation responses

practice.analogy: Instead of searching a pile of case files for a sentence, you first draw the map of who is connected to whom, write a one-page brief for each cluster, and read the briefs to answer big-picture questions.

library.name: graphrag
library.what: Microsoft’s open-source GraphRAG: indexing pipeline plus local and global search, driven by a CLI and settings.yaml.

practice.note: Set your model API key in the .env file created by init. Indexing calls the LLM for every chunk, so try a small sample first. Command options can change between versions; check graphrag --help.

samples.code:
import subprocess, pathlib

root = pathlib.Path("sahayak")
(root / "input").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
for p in sorted(pathlib.Path("reports").glob("*.txt"))[:200]:      # sample first
    (root / "input" / p.name).write_text(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), encoding="utf-8")

subprocess.run(["graphrag", "init", "--root", str(root)], check=True)
subprocess.run(["graphrag", "index", "--root", str(root)], check=True)

for method, q in [("local", "Which vendors are linked to repeated outages in Pune circle?"),
                  ("global", "What are the main causes of customer complaints?")]:
    r = subprocess.run(["graphrag", "query", "--root", str(root), "--method", method, "--query", q],
                       capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
    print(method.upper(), r.stdout[:600], sep="\n")

interview.question: How does GraphRAG differ from vector RAG?
interview.answer: Vector RAG retrieves chunks similar to the question. GraphRAG first extracts entities and relationships into a graph, clusters it into communities with summaries, and answers multi-hop questions by walking the graph and whole-corpus questions by combining community summaries.

interview.question: When is GraphRAG not worth it?
interview.answer: When most questions are single-fact lookups that vector RAG already answers, or the corpus changes too fast to re-index affordably.
